title: Learn a tiny image classifier by doing

paper.name: Illustrative paper: CNN image classification (demo)
paper.one_line: A convolutional network classifies everyday objects; the paper reports accuracy on a large labeled set.

core_method.what_they_did: Train a neural classifier on labeled images, then assign each new image to the class with the highest predicted score.
core_method.inputs: RGB images and class labels (e.g. cat vs dog vs car).
core_method.how_results: Compare predicted labels to ground truth; report overall accuracy and per-class errors.
from_paper: Classification = map an input image to a discrete class label.
Performance is judged by how often the predicted label matches the true label.
Hard examples and mistakes matter for understanding the method.

teaching_simplifications: We do not train a CNN here — that needs more compute and paper detail than this prototype uses.
Each “image” is shown as a small feature card with two numbers: brightness and edge-ness (0–10).
Classification uses nearest class prototype (1-NN to class centers) — same decide-a-label idea, much simpler math.
Only eight toy samples so you can see every prediction by hand.

exercise.goal: Classify each sample by finding the nearest class prototype, then check which ones you (and the method) got right.

samples.label: A
samples.hint: Bright and smooth — should sit near class A.

samples.label: B
samples.hint: Dark with strong edges — near B.

samples.label: C
samples.hint: Middle of both axes — near C.

samples.label: A
samples.hint: Borderline — still closer to A than B/C for this demo.

steps: Look at the three class prototypes (centers) on the feature map.
For each sample, measure distance to each prototype (Euclidean in 2D).
Assign the label of the nearest prototype — that is the model’s prediction.
Compare prediction to the true label; mark hits and misses.
Read the explanation: why misses happen near boundaries, and how this mirrors the paper’s error analysis idea.

explanations.after_run: You just ran the same high-level loop the paper describes: take an input, produce a class, score against truth. The paper uses a deep net and pixels; here the “net” is nearest prototype on two hand-built features.
explanations.mistakes: Mistakes usually sit near the boundary between two class centers — the same intuition as confusing classes in a real classifier’s confusion matrix.
explanations.paper_link: In the paper, accuracy summarizes many such decisions. Studying individual errors (as you did) is how researchers interpret what the method still gets wrong.

challenge.title: Challenge: flip a prediction
challenge.prompt: Sample s7 is labeled A. Drag its brightness or edge-ness (or type new values) until the nearest prototype becomes B or C. Then run again.
challenge.success: You moved the sample across a decision boundary. In the paper’s world, that is like changing the image enough that the model’s top class flips — useful intuition before you touch real training code.

from_paper: Classify inputs into discrete labels and measure accuracy / errors.
simplified_for_teaching: Prototype nearest-neighbor instead of a trained CNN
Eight samples instead of a full benchmark
